newsitem.title: USA: Plaintiffs in Florida suit denounce tobacco talks.
newsitem.headline: Plaintiffs in Florida suit denounce tobacco talks.

text.p: Plaintiffs in a Florida case involving the effects of secondhand smoke on Tuesday denounced the so-called "global settlement" talks, fearing the tobacco industry has stepped up the negotiations to avoid their landmark case.

According to comments from state officials involved in the negotiations with tobacco companies, the talks have been stepped up recently and could lead to a broad settlement of tobacco-related litigation within weeks.

Plaintiffs in the class-action trial scheduled to begin June 2 in Miami, in which non-smoking flight attendants are seeking damages for illnesses they say were caused by secondhand smoke, said they suspected a link between the stepped-up talks and the imminent start of their trial.

"Certainly there is no compelling reason to have this settled this week," Norma Broin, lead plaintiff in the suit, told a news conference. Broin, who never smoked, decided to file the suit after surviving a bout of lung cancer, now in remission.

"We are quite frankly suspicious that a plan is in the works to prevent our national class action on behalf of 60,000 flight attendants to go to trial on Monday," Stanley Rosenblatt, an attorney for the class, told the news conference. "It's no coincidence...that the so-called global settlement negotiations are becoming intense and that these people are meeting every day," he said.
Rosenblatt has said he is seeking $5 billion or more in damages in the case, the first lawsuit related to secondhand smoke and the first class-action case against tobacco that would go to trial.

Rosenblatt said he expected the tobacco industry, after reaching a settlement, to go to a "friendly" federal judge and obtain a temporary injunction that would stop his case, known Broin vs. Philip Morris Cos Inc.
But he said, even if such an order were issued, he would expect Dade County Circuit Judge Robert Kaye, who is hearing the suit, to disregard it and allow the flight attendants' case to proceed.

Of the attorney generals and others involved in the global settlement talks, ostensibly on the side of anyone making claims against tobacco, he said, "How dare they presume to negotiate and reach a settlement on behalf of clients they've never met."
Rosenblatt also said the American Lung Association and the Boston University School of Public Health were opposing the global settlement talks.

Rosenblatt and his wife Susan also represent some 500,000 Florida smokers in Engle vs. R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a class-action lawsuit scheduled for trial September 8. But he said they were not involved in the industry settlement talks.
"We are so far out of the loop that we might as well be on Mars," Rosenblatt said. However, he added, "I'm very proud not to be part of that loop because I'm highly suspicious of it," he said.

Tobacco industry attorneys in Miami for pretrial hearings in advance of the Broin case, declined comment on remarks made during the news conference, which was held less than a week before jury selection was due to begin.

The judge has stopped short of issuing a gag order connected with the case, but he has ruled to deny media access to depositions and exhibits and has repeatedly warned all the attorneys to be "circumspect" in their dealings with the news media.
Philip Morris Cos Inc, maker of Marlboro, is the largest U.S. tobacco company, with about 48 percent of the market for cigarettes. R.J. Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
